messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 42-year-old ship captain who has spent two decades navigating the Atlantic, a career that once gave him a profound sense of mastery and control. That changed eighteen months ago, when his cargo vessel was caught in a coordinated pirate attack off the coast of West Africa. He remembers the sequence with unbearable clarity: the warning shots fired across his bow, the explosion that tore through the engine room, and then the boarding—masked men in military-style uniforms throwing crew members to the deck, screaming orders in a language he couldn't understand. He watched a first mate take a rifle butt to the skull for hesitating. By the time naval forces arrived, three of his men were dead. Marcus was praised for his composure during the crisis, but privately, he had already begun to unravel.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself unable to shake the certainty that the people responsible had faced no consequences—the attackers had melted back into the coastal chaos, untouchable, unpunished. This belief that justice had failed hardened into something darker: a conviction that he could not rely on anyone else to keep him or his crew safe. He started to see threats everywhere. A delivery truck backfiring on the dock sent him diving for cover. When a deckhand playfully tossed a coil of rope across the hold, Marcus felt his chest seize with the old terror of objects being thrown. He began scanning every face on the pier for signs of danger, reading aggressive intent into ordinary gestures. The world had become a place where violence could erupt without warning, and he was certain that if he let his guard down for even a moment, he would be caught unprepared again.

This hypervigilance toward people became exhausting, but Marcus could not stop. He started choosing his seat in restaurants and at the union hall based on how safe it felt—always with his back to a wall, always facing the door, always calculating escape routes. At home, he struggled to fall asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening for sounds that shouldn't be there. His wife found him pacing the bedroom at 3 a.m., insisting he'd heard something outside. His vigilance also fed his sense of isolation: the more he scanned for threats, the more convinced he became that he was the only one paying attention, the only one who understood how dangerous people really were. Every near-miss, every unexplained sound, every uniformed figure in his peripheral vision seemed to confirm that his distrust was justified.

To manage this overwhelming sense of danger, Marcus developed strategies that only deepened his problems. He began avoiding unfamiliar places entirely, sticking to routes and ports he knew well, refusing charters that would take him into new waters where he couldn't assess the risks. At work, he started dropping important responsibilities—delegating safety inspections to his second mate, skipping the captain's mandatory log reviews, canceling crew meetings because being in a room full of people felt too exposed. When he wasn't working, he turned to gambling, spending long nights at offshore poker tables where the noise and distraction let him forget the memories for a few hours. But each loss at the table, each responsibility he abandoned, only reinforced his belief that he was falling apart, that he couldn't handle his own life. He would think: *If I think about what happened, I'll never get through the day.* So he pushed the memories down, and they came back harder.

The cycle tightened over the months. His avoidance of unfamiliar places meant he turned down a promotion that would have required him to oversee a new shipping route. His wife stopped inviting him to social events because he would either cancel last minute or sit in silence, watching the exits. She told him he wasn't the same man she married—and she was right. Marcus knew he was losing his grip, but he could not see a way out. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment on the bridge last week, when a faulty pressure valve released a loud bang that sounded exactly like the explosion he remembered. He dropped to his knees, shaking, in front of his entire crew. The humiliation was absolute, but it was also the first time he admitted to himself that he could not keep living this way. He is afraid of what therapy will unearth—convinced, in fact, that talking about the event will break him completely. But he is also terrified of what he will become if he does not try.
